title: The Temple's Fall and Staying Ready
overview: Looking at the temple, Jesus predicts its destruction, then warns his followers about war, persecution and false messiahs, speaks of the coming of the Son of Man, and urges them to stay alert.

parts.label: The temple will fall (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: King Herod had rebuilt the temple on a grand scale with huge stones, yet Jesus says every one will be thrown down. Roman forces destroyed it in AD 70, about forty years later; here four disciples ask him privately when this will happen and what sign will warn them.

parts.label: Hard times, not yet the end (vv. 5-13)
parts.note: Pretenders claiming his name, wars, earthquakes and famines are compared to the first pains of childbirth: real suffering, but only the start. His followers will be beaten in synagogues (Jewish meeting places), tried before rulers and even betrayed by family, yet the Holy Spirit will give them words, and whoever holds on to the end will be saved.

parts.label: The warning sign and flight (vv. 14-20)
parts.note: The sign is a phrase from Daniel for a detestable thing that defiles the temple and brings ruin, first used of a pagan altar set up there in 167 BC; many link it here to Rome's war on Jerusalem in AD 66 to 70, others to a future event. Scholars debate whether the aside to the reader is a nudge to Mark's first audience or a pointer back to Daniel, but the command is plain: flee at once, in days so terrible that God cuts them short for the sake of his chosen people.

parts.label: False messiahs, the true coming (vv. 21-27)
parts.note: Jesus says not to believe anyone pointing to a messiah here or there, then speaks of a darkened sun and falling stars, language Isaiah used for the fall of empires, which some read as picture language and others as literal signs. The Son of Man (Jesus' title for himself) coming on the clouds echoes Daniel 7, where a human figure receives power from God; most Christians read this as his return at the end of history, while some see it fulfilled in Jerusalem's fall.

parts.label: The fig tree lesson (vv. 28-31)
parts.note: Just as new fig leaves show that summer is close, these events will show that what he has described is near. Readers differ on 'this generation': many take it to mean Jesus' own hearers, some of whom lived to see Jerusalem fall, while others take it to mean the people alive when the final signs appear.

parts.label: No one knows the hour (vv. 32-37)
parts.note: Jesus says no one knows the day, not even the Son, only the Father, a line Christians have long discussed and often explain as him speaking within the limits of his human life. The owner who gives each servant a task and may come home in any watch of the night means stay awake and keep at your work, and Christians read the owner as Jesus himself.

disagreement: Christians genuinely differ on what this chapter predicts: some say nearly all of it came true when Jerusalem fell in AD 70, many say it blends that event with a still future return of Jesus, and others read much of it as describing the end of history yet to come.
think: What in your life feels as solid as those temple stones, and what would be left if it fell?
